questions.q: Per this lesson, what should happen before you ever open App Manager to build an app?
options: Nothing — you should start building immediately to save time
Writing the Apex classes the app will eventually need
Gathering requirements: who, what, why, and scale
Assigning all user profiles access to every object
questions.explain: The four questions — who, what, why, and scale — turn a vague ask into a real requirement before any configuration starts.

questions.q: In the declarative-first design order, what comes before building a custom object?
options: Writing an Apex trigger
Assigning page layouts
Creating a custom Lightning component
Checking whether a standard object already covers the requirement
questions.explain: The reuse check — does a standard object already fit — always comes before building anything custom.

questions.q: In the design order from this lesson, what comes before customizing with Lightning components?
options: Configuring with fields, page layouts, and Flow
Writing Apex
Nothing — components always come first
Deploying with change sets
questions.explain: Configure (declarative tools like fields, layouts, Flow) before you customize (components), and customize before Apex.

questions.q: In the warranty-claims worked example, why was a master-detail relationship chosen between Claim and Asset instead of a lookup?
options: Master-detail is always the default choice regardless of the business rule
A claim can't exist without its asset — the business rule demanded the tighter relationship
Lookups aren't supported on custom objects
It was an arbitrary choice with no business justification
questions.explain: The relationship type should come from the business rule — here, a claim logically can't exist independent of its asset.

questions.q: Why does this lesson favor the "most declarative solution that satisfies the requirement" over a more impressive custom build?
options: Declarative solutions are always faster to build, with no other benefit
Apex is not allowed on the Salesforce platform
Declarative solutions cannot be tested
Less to maintain, less to break, and easier for the next admin to understand
questions.explain: The lesson explains that minimal, declarative solutions reduce long-term maintenance and hand-off risk — not just build time.
